world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Leenhardt, Maurice 1946, Langues et dialectes de l'Austro-Melanesie (697pp; only description per Glottolog); not accessible online.

new_statements.quote: [p. 25] § 2. — Accent et ton. Accent comme celui de l'AJIË. Tous les phonèmes sont très nasalisés. Tons analogues à ceux de l'AJIË et du BOEWE. — [p. 13, Ajië § 2, the statement referred to:] Dans les termes dissyllabiques ou monosyllabiques il y a un accent tonique léger sur la dernière syllabe du mot plein. Dans les composés, le mot plein garde l'accent, qu'il soit en position initiale ou finale. [...] Mais il arrive, dans certains mots de trois syllabes ayant trois voyelles similaires, que le mot se prononce sans accent aucun : kororo = déchet de pierre.
new_statements.translation: [p. 25] § 2. Accent and tone. Accent like that of Ajië. All the phonemes are strongly nasalised. Tones analogous to those of Ajië and Boewe. — [p. 13, Ajië § 2:] In disyllabic or monosyllabic terms there is a light tonic accent on the last syllable of the full (lexical) word. In compounds, the full word keeps the accent, whether it is in initial or final position. [...] But it happens, in certain three-syllable words having three similar vowels, that the word is pronounced with no accent at all: kororo = stone chippings.
new_statements.citation: Leenhardt, Maurice. 1946. Langues et dialectes de l'Austro-Mélanésie (Travaux et Mémoires de l'Institut d'Ethnologie 46). Paris: Institut d'Ethnologie. XLVIII+676 pp. Chapter "2. — Arhâ", I. Phonétique, § 2 Accent et ton, p. 25 (Gallica ark:/12148/bpt6k21694f, view f72); the referenced Ajië statement is chapter "1. Ajië", § 2, p. 13 (view f60).
new_statements.locator: p. 25, § 2 'Accent et ton' (Gallica view f72); reference statement p. 13, § 2 (view f60)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Read by eye (Leenhardt 1946 p. 25, running head "GROUPE DU SUD : ARHÂ"): "§ 2. — Accent et ton. Accent comme celui de l'AJIË. Tous les phonèmes sont très nasalisés. / Tons analogues à ceux de l'AJIË et du BOEWE." is there verbatim, followed by II. MOTS §3 (words end in an open vowel; composition as in Ajië; "L'AJIË domine dans ce dialecte"). p. 13, "GROUPE DU SUD : AJIË", § 2 Accent et ton) carries verbatim "Dans les termes dissyllabiques ou monosyllabiques il y a un accent tonique léger sur la dernière syllabe du mot plein. Dans les composés, le mot plein garde l'accent, qu'il soit en position initiale ou finale." and "Mais il arrive, dans certains mots de trois syllabes ayant trois voyell…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Leenhardt gives no independent rule for Arhâ: he states that its accent is the same as Ajië's, which he describes as a light tonic accent on the final syllable of the lexical ('full') word, kept on the lexical word in compounds whether that word comes first or last. Taken at face value this is final-syllable word stress. He also claims Arhâ has 'tones' like Ajië and Boewe (four pitch levels in his Ajië notice).
new_statements.exceptions: By reference to Ajië only: some trisyllables with three identical vowels are said to be pronounced without any accent (kororo). Nothing Arhâ-specific.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain = the 'mot plein' (lexical word), including compounds; the tone remark is word-level (minimal pairs in Ajië). Caveats that make the reading low-confidence: (1) the Arhâ statement is a one-line cross-reference, not an observation on Arhâ words; (2) Leenhardt's Ajië description was later superseded: de la Fontinelle 1976 (La langue de Houaïlou) describes an intensity/glottalised accent that is normally on the initial syllable (ajie1238 audit, snippet notes p. 126 'accent n'est pas sur l'initiale dans certains cas'), and Haudricourt (BSL 69(2), 1974) and Rivierre (BSL 73(1), 1978, pp. 416, 429) treat the southern group as non-tonal accent languages, so Leenhardt's 'tons' are not musical tone; (3) identity of Leenhardt's ARHÂ vs modern aqr/aok is uncertain (see identity_note). Reading 'tonal-with-stress-statement' would also fit the source's own wording; 'fixed-final' records the stress-placement claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Leenhardt 1946 (the only description; Glottolog's MED for arha1237) labels as "ARHÂ" the speech of Nérin, Wendji (Ouendji) and Monfaoué (Montfaoué), "entre Houailou et Poya", 150 people (p. 24), and as "ARO" that of Poya, Nékliai, Kareji (Kradji), Goapoin and Netéa, 300 people (p. 29). Modern sources (ALK; fr Wikipedia for both aqr and aok) place Arhâ [aqr, arha1237] at Nékliaï and Kradji, i.e. the villages Leenhardt assigns to ARO (= Arhö, arho1237 [aok]). The mapping of Leenhardt's two labels onto the two ISO codes is therefore uncertain; the quoted statement is Leenhardt's ARHÂ notice. His ARO notice (p. 29) contains no accent rule at all.
